topics.title: A Quick Word
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 1 - Introduction/Academy - Intro 1 - A Quick Word.txt

blocks.text: A majority of the content throughout this manual will serve to provide a conceptual framework behind our methodology...basically informing us of the "why" behind everything. As with any area of study, having a sound understanding of the concepts involved will facilitate the application, or the "how". In other words, if you understand what we're trying to accomplish with our protocol and why, you will be better equipped to instruct and teach our clients while providing a safer and more meaningful experience.

Having said that, the most fruitful path to becoming a top level MaxStrength Fitness Life Transformer will be a combination of reading, shadowing, training (i.e. working out), and hands-on practice (equipment set up and instruction). Now there is no specific order or formula to these elements as each individual will benefit from a different combination but it will be in your best interest to continuously cycle through these as you progress through the on-boarding process. Even as you begin supervising your own sessions it would be in your best interest to continue to study the material in the Academy and elsewhere. The learning process does not stop once we begin training clients. The reading will make more sense once you've done some shadowing and the shadowing and reading will make more sense once you've experienced the hands-on training and vice versa.

The MaxStength Fitness Leadership Team will help guide you through these initial phases and will be with you throughout your career. We will continually strive to become the foremost experts in strength training as we look to deliver the most efficient, effective, and safe resistance exercise program available. We will pride ourselves on attentive, meaningful, and concise instruction based on a well informed understanding of the physiology of strength training. This is truly what separates us from other trainers in the industry and will continue to be our competitive advantage!

A glossary of terms follows in the next step as a high level introduction to some of the language used in the Academy and in our day to day practice as instructors. This next step will also serve as a quick reference guide to help understand the terms as you go through the on-boarding process.

The following terms are used throughout the MaxStrength Fitness Academy and used by us throughout our day as Exercise Practitioners. It is therefore imperative for new team members to learn these EXACT terms and concepts and be comfortable using them during the on-boarding process and beyond. There are a lot of commonly held misconceptions used to talk about and describe exercise. In some cases it may be necessary for new team members to "unlearn" these misconceptions. We have a precise (and more accurate) way of understanding, discussing, and instructing exercise, and this is the language we use.

This also impacts our choice of words used to refer to our profession. Exercise Practitioner, Exercise Instructor (Instructor), Life Transformer, Strength Training Specialist (Strength Trainer or Trainer) are all acceptable descriptors for how we see ourselves and for what we do at MaxStrength Fitness. In an attempt to distinguish ourselves from an unqualified and over-saturated industry, we intentionally try to avoid titles like "Personal Trainer".

Assumed vs. Real Objective (of exercise) - arguably the most pervasive and most negatively impactful beliefs about resistance training is centered around the objective of resistance training itself. It seems to be widely accepted that the objective or goal of a strength training session (or set) should be to lift more weight for more reps, or to increase in some quantitative measure. When in reality, the objective should be to attempt to increase the stimulus achieved during a set of resistance training. This can occur as a result of lifting more weight or performing more reps but only if the quality of the execution of the exercise is maintained or improved upon. The stimulus we seek is an internal physiological response to the mechanical tension experienced during a physical effort and not necessarily dependent on external factors such as weight and reps. In other words, more weight or more reps do not automatically equal more stimulus. If there is more momentum present or the trainee is altering their form to lift the weight, the stimulus (tension) experienced by the targeted muscles is decreased. Intentional execution with a focus on control will create a safer and more effective stimulus. See also Progressive Overload and Intent.

Bone Density (Remodeling) - Bone remodeling is a dynamic process that involves the continuous renewal of bone tissue, influenced significantly by resistance training. When we engage in resistance exercise, the mechanical tension experienced by the muscle fibers is transferred as stress to the involved bones. This stress stimulates bone-forming cells called osteoblasts. These cells respond to the increased load by producing new bone matrix, thereby enhancing bone density and strength. Thus, resistance training not only enhances muscular strength but also plays a crucial role in fortifying the bones against the strains of daily activities and aging.

Concentric - the positive or lifting phase of a repetition (i.e. the actual lifting of the weight). During this phase, a muscle contracts or shortens, exerting a pulling force on the bones, to produce mechanical tension and ultimately movement about the joint(s) on which the muscle(s) acts. This concentric portion of a repetition is also the more challenging phase of the movement. In other words, a subject will always be able to lower more weight than they will be able to lift. This is an inherent safety mechanism in the body and is due to the friction in the overlapping or cross-bridging of the actin and myosin components of a shortened muscle fiber.

Continuous - the name of the protocol used to describe the technique or approach to resistance training used at MaxStrength Fitness is the Continuous Tension Method. Simply stated, once a set of exercise has begun, the musculature is under load and there are no points during the set where the muscles are unloaded (i.e. there is no rest). We seek to maintain continuous tension of the targeted muscle(s) for the duration of the set or until the subject reaches their maximum tolerable effort.

Contract(ion) - the muscular action whereby the actin and myosin components of a muscle fiber connect, overlap, and pull creating an overlapping or shortening of the muscle. This muscle shortening exerts a pulling force on the bones of the body and creates movement (or attempted movement). Muscular contractions are technically explained by the sliding filament theory in physiology. See also Concentric.

Eccentric - the negative or lowering phase of a repetition (i.e. lowering of the weight). During this phase, the contracted muscle begins to uncouple or lengthen. It is important to note that even though the muscle is lengthening during an eccentric action, there is still a contraction present and therefore tension is being produced. This is a result of the actin and myosin of the muscle fibers attempting to maintain their overlap while gradually releasing their connections. This is what gives control to the movement as opposed to just allowing the weight to free fall in the absence of force. Additionally, because the eccentric phase requires a lower level of effort, it will feel easier to the subject. This will likely cause the subject to unknowingly take longer during the eccentric to rest or to limit discomfort. As a result, the instructor must be aware of this tendency and encourage the subject to maintain a constant pace throughout the movement.

Exercise Induced Headache (EIH) - Rare phenomenon where a small percentage of clients will get a strong headache during a set of exercise, usually the leg press. They are commonly described as originating in the back of the head/neck area, and if the effort continues, the pain makes its way to the front of the head, forming around one eye. Any occurrence of an EIH should be met with an abundance of caution and the client should stop the exercise immediately. Only resume when it has completely diminished. See the EIH module in the "Exercise Performance" section of the Academy for more guidance.

Failure (Fatigue) - the ultimate or eventual goal of most or our exercises. Traditionally, failure has been thought of as a mechanical term describing the inability of the involved muscles to continue to lift the load in a given exercise due to a mechanism of fatigue. But more realistically the inability to continue to produce effort comes down to the subject reaching what is known as their Maximum Tolerable Perception of Effort. Essentially, the subject will choose to stop lifting a weight due to discomfort or perceived exertion prior to actual muscular failure. This is more accurately termed as "task failure," which is the inability to continue a task, and is the most common type of "movement failure". Basically, subjects will voluntarily cease an exercise without having fully exhausted their true physical capabilities because of the perceived level of effort. While this is not necessarily optimal for strength training, it can still be stimulative and most importantly is an ability that can be improved upon over the course of a subject's resistance training career. When exposed to these stresses/sensations, we become more tolerant of them.

Fatigue - having to do with a muscle's temporary and reversible reduction in exercise performance resulting from a previous bout of exercise. This is an objective measurement and when constructing an exercise program, every measure should be made to minimize the fatigue during the session as well as fatigue that is carried over from one session to the next. This is affected by a myriad of factors including but not limited to a trainee's experience level, current state of recovery from previous workout, discomfort experienced during current workout, perceived exertion, muscular soreness, and momentary weakening during an exercise (reduced MUR caused by calcium ion influx). Fatigue in this case does not refer to a subject's lack of readiness or energy levels. Any level of physiological fatigue present will act to decrease motor unit recruitment and mechanical tension thereby inhibiting the potential stimulative effect of resistance training. Each repetition of an exercise has an unavoidable "fatigue cost," and because of this, more reps (and more sets) will result in a higher level of physiological fatigue. This is a primary justification in support of a low volume, high intensity approach, which is the foundation of the MSF Continuous Tension protocol. Not to mention that higher reps and volume also lends itself to muscle fiber damage and inflammation which are inhibitory to the hypertrophy process. Similarly, exercises that emphasize an excessively lengthened (i.e. stretched) muscle position will create more fatigue than exercises that emphasize shortened positions.

Force - In physics, force is an influence tending to change the motion of a body or produce motion in a stationary body. The magnitude is calculated by multiplying the mass of the body by its acceleration. For our purposes, force can be explained simply as using one's physical strength against a resistance or simply stated as effort.

Force-Velocity Relationship - describes how a muscle's ability to produce force changes depending on the contraction velocity of the muscle fibers involved. In simple terms, when a muscle contracts quickly it produces less force per fiber. When a muscle contracts slowly, especially when involuntarily slow due to heavier loads and fatigue, it can produce more force. Only with a high level of effort (MUR) and an involuntarily slow contraction speed (Mechanical Tension) do we have the potential for a stimulative set of resistance training, especially the more/longer one trains. Keep in mind that with novice strength trainers, almost any level of effort can be stimulative because it is more than they are accustomed to.

Frequency - how often a workout takes place or more specifically, how often a muscle group (and more specifically muscle fiber) is trained, usually referring to a weekly time period. Most of our clients will train most of their muscle groups twice per week.

Gradual - taking place slowly or by degrees or increments. More specifically, when applying force to begin an exercise, it is our objective to do so gradually. So to begin pushing (exerting force) at a level lower than that required to move the selected load and incrementally push harder over time until movement occurs (i.e. the weight is lifted). This is one of the more important concepts that a trainee should understand and practice to perfect. Therefore, the instructor must fully understand this concept and be able to describe and observe that this is happening.

High Intensity - in the fitness realm, this descriptor refers to a type of exercise that is of a high level of effort. By definition, a high intensity activity cannot be carried out for a long period of time. To say it another way, the higher the level of effort, the briefer the duration that that activity can be carried out. This is to distinguish such an activity from lower level activities that most will identify with exercise, including walking, jogging, or aerobics. The Continuous Tension protocol used at MaxStrength Fitness is considered high intensity resistance training.

Inroad - the depth of momentary fatigue in a muscle or muscle group attained due to exercise. Keep in mind that while fatigue itself is not the stimulus we seek from exercise, it is an unavoidable byproduct of muscular work and mechanical tension. Inroad or fatigue is often used to explain the real objective of exercise but a more accurate description of the desired effect is the mechanical tension experienced by the working muscles.

Intensity - Intensity merely indicates how hard the muscular work or the degree of difficulty in the execution of an exercise. In general, the effectiveness of the muscular growth stimulus appears to be directly proportional to the intensity of muscular work (effort) during exercise.

Intent (Purpose) - In general terms, a trainee's true instinctive objective during a set of resistance training. This seems rather simple and straightforward on the surface but further introspection will reveal that for most trainee's, their intent is incongruent with that which leads to optimal results from resistance training. More than likely, a client's instincts will override their intent. This will turn into a desire to either keep the machine moving to "get more reps" or to altogether quit because they "can't get another rep." It's either a quantitative goal of getting more or a protective mechanism resulting from fight or flight while under duress. As a MSF Exercise Practitioner, there is an obligation to continually remind the client of the real objective of exercise and that their intent should be to create as much tension on the targeted muscle as possible. Proper intention will drive the behavior of the trainee and the execution of the exercise. On a more narrowly focused level, intent refers to a subject's desire to move faster on an exercise where fatigue is accumulating and therefore slowing, in an effort to maintain one's pace. See also Assumed vs. Real Objective and Speed.

Length-Tension Relationship - explains how a muscle fiber's ability to produce force changes depending on how stretched (lengthened) or contracted (shortened) it is. In simple terms, if a muscle is fully contracted or fully stretched, its force producing capabilities are diminished. This has to do with how a muscle fiber's actin and myosin heads overlap. When a muscle fiber is in the mid-to-long length position there is an optimal overlap and ideal leverage for them to grab and pull across each other (contract) most effectively. This helps to explain why we are stronger in certain points of a range of motion of an exercise than others.

Lower Turnaround (Lower Turn/Bottom) - the specific point in the execution of an exercise occurring at the end of the eccentric, or lowering phase, of the range of motion. The term "lower" is in reference to the position of the weight stack as it is being lowered. This is not to be confused with the position of the body during the movement. For example in the pulldown exercise, the lower turnaround would be when the arms (and movement arm of the machine) are at the highest point, further from the body. But this is the lower turnaround on this exercise because it is the end of the eccentric phase and the weight stack will be at its lowermost point.

Momentary Muscular Failure - training to the point where positive (concentric) movement is no longer possible due to the subject having reached their Maximum Tolerable Perception of Effort. This is also where the instructor would stop their count of the repetitions as only full reps, with full ROM and in the prescribed form are recorded. See also Failure and Fatigue for more. Using the term “Full Effort” can be seen as a more user friendly way to discuss this with a client.

Motor Unit Recruitment (MUR) - a physiological process whereby the nervous system activates any number of motor units and the muscle fibers they innervate to meet a given level of effort from a working muscle. Not all motor units in a muscle are recruited during movement or exertion, only those required to complete the task. As the intensity of effort increases, so does motor unit recruitment (i.e. more muscle fibers are activated or innervated). They are also recruited in an orderly fashion, according to Henneman’s Size Principle, from the smallest, lower force producing fibers to the largest, higher force producing fibers depending on the momentary effort required. In order for a muscle fiber to be stimulated, it must first be activated/recruited. Importantly, if we are to create an adaptive stimulus from our resistance training, a higher level of motor unit recruitment would stimulate more muscle. Therefore, a higher level of effort is recommended as a way to elicit a stronger response from the training.

Movement Pattern - a general descriptor for the path of motion required by the joints of the body on a given exercise. Examples of upper body movement patterns would be calling a chest press a horizontal push or a pull down a vertical pull. Or even more generally a "push" or a "pull". A lower body example would be calling a leg press a squat pattern or referring to a leg curl as knee flexion.

Negative - a less formal way to describe the lowering or eccentric phase of an exercise. Lowering the weight, as it refers to the weight stack, is the ‘negative’ phase of a repetition. Opposite of the lifting or positive phase of a repetition. Importantly, it requires less effort than the concentric phase and instructors should ensure subjects do not linger or stall during the eccentric phase. They should maintain the same pace throughout the movement. See also Eccentric.

Neural Adaptations - Initially, strength improvements on a given exercise or movement are largely attributed to enhanced communication and coordination between the brain and the muscles. This process involves increased efficiency in the recruitment of motor units, which are the nerve cells that signal a group of muscle fibers to contract. As you continue to train/practice a movement pattern, your central nervous system becomes better at activating a greater number of motor units simultaneously, thereby improving coordination and force output. These neural adaptations will necessarily precede the muscular adaptations that are the desired stimulus from resistance training. It is also important to note that neural adaptations usually occur relatively quickly and can actually happen rep to rep. It may only take a few workouts (i.e. sets) on a specific exercise to become neurologically proficient especially with a more stable, linear, bilateral movement pattern. For instance, the motor pattern for a leg press is more easily learned and adapted to than a dumbell lateral raise. See also Motor Unit Recruitment.

Pace - Refers to the speed of movement of an exercise. Our Continuous Tension Protocol dictates that a continuous, steady pace of approximately 6 to 10 seconds be employed for all movements. Furthermore, the established speed should not change unless instructed. This means lifting and lowering the resistance with the same speed. So if we lift the weight in 8 seconds, we should attempt to lower the weight in 8 seconds. The primary consideration for this exaggerated control is to ensure safety above all else. Sudden movement or rapid acceleration introduces excessive and potentially dangerous forces. Acceleration also reduces single fiber mechanical tension and therefore reduces the desired stimulus. Along with Posture, Path, and Purpose, Pace is part of the "4 P's" that an instructor should look for when observing and instructing a set of exercise. See also Speed.

Path - Refers to the line of travel of a limb or other body part on an exercise. For example, when performing a chest press exercise, what path are the arms (i.e. elbows) moving through? Because the shoulders and hands are fixed, the elbows are somewhat "free to float". We should seek consistent and symmetrical paths of movement on every exercise. Oftentimes when fatigue sets in, a trainee will change their arm path in an effort to keep the machine moving. Along with Posture, Pace, and Purpose, Path is part of the "4 P's" that an instructor should look for when observing and instructing a set of exercise.

Pelvic Tilt - the result of either contracting the abdominal muscles or extending the spine (lifting the chest). A posterior pelvic tilt is achieved by contracting the abdomen and rounding the spine. An anterior pelvic tilt occurs when the back is arched and the chest is lifted. During an anterior pelvic tilt the abdominal muscles are stretched or elongated. For most of the exercises performed, there will be a required posterior or anterior pelvic tilt required. This is a major component of the posture we refer to when instructing or describing an exercise.

Positive - a less formal way to describe the lifting or concentric phase of an exercise. Lifting the weight as it refers to the weight stack is the positive component of a repetition. Opposite of the lowering or negative phase of a repetition. See also Concentric.

Posture - how the client is expected to sit or position themselves on an exercise. And for most exercises, the trainee is expected to maintain this positioning at all times. Without establishing and maintaining a proper posture, the trainee will not be able to meaningfully direct their effort at a stimulative level. Exceptions to maintaining a posture would include the Lumbar Extension or Abdominal where the torso is expected to move and change positions during the exercise. But in these cases, there are still positional cues that should be given to ensure proper execution. The instructor should know how to properly position the client, instruct them how exactly to hold their posture, and watch for any form discrepancies during the set. Along with Pace and Path, Posture is part of the "4 P's" that an instructor should look for when observing and instructing a set of exercise.

Progressive Overload - a commonly misunderstood and misused term in the fitness community, Progressive Overload is NOT the idea that one should lift more weight or perform more reps or more sets in order to create a stimulus (i.e. get stronger). Instead, Progressive Overload is evidence that one has gotten stronger by the ability to perform more reps with the same weight or more weight for the same reps, under the SAME conditions. That last part is critical in that all conditions must be the same in order for the increased strength to be demonstrated. It must be the same exercise, at the same point in the workout (or at least not directly affected by the exercises before it), with the same settings, and using similar form and execution. If any of these other variables change, it may be a result of these changes that one appears to have gotten stronger. Importantly, as instructors, we should be fully informed on this and other fitness concepts but it may not be in our best interest as a business to discuss the actual weight and reps achieved by our clients. Our instruction and communication with our clients should be focused on more of a qualitative approach and less about the quantity. Yes, we want to encourage a high level of effort, and we'd like for our clients to get objectively stronger, but not without and emphasis on perfect form. An occasional acknowledgement of having increased the weight if the client asks is probably harmless, but be careful not to make these discussions a habit or to encourage chasing reps or weights. This will almost always result in the client pursuing the "assumed objective" which leads to improper and unsafe form.

Purpose - The 4th and final P in our MSF Instructor "cheat sheet" is Purpose. This may very well be the missing ingredient to most attempts at a productive and successful exercise intervention. Purpose is essentially addressing the question, 'what is the primary or immediate goal of our set of an exercise?'. Most clients are simply trying to last as long as the trainer is requiring of them. Their instinctive mindset is that the workout is being done to them. The correct technical answer to the question 'what is the immediate goal of the workout?' is to increase Motor Unit Recruitment (MUR). Increasing MUR leads to a greater number of muscle fibers exposed to mechanical tension, which creates a more meaningful stimulus. In order to increase MUR, one would need to increase their momentary effort or simply train harder. So 'purpose' here is best described as the intent of the trainee to train with more effort, or to challenge themselves more, with each subsequent workout or set. Rather than having the trainer deliver the workout to them, the client should be an active participant with a long term goal of training harder. The instructor is there to help them learn and practice this most valuable skill.

Range of Motion (ROM) - can refer to both the distance of travel or excursion of a machine and the distance that the joints/limbs/torso of the trainee move during an exercise. In general, it is important to note that more range of motion is not necessarily better or more desirable. With safety our main priority, the instructor must ensure that the range of motion established is conservative, tolerable, and tailored to every individual client on every exercise. These concepts are discussed throughout the Academy and the onboarding process, as well as throughout the instructor's career as MSF.

Speed - a relative term usually referring to the actual pace of execution of an exercise. In the "fitness world," the speed we use at MSF of 6 to 10 seconds to lift the weight and 6 - 10 seconds to lower would be considered slow. While this may be an accurate depiction, it is necessary to ensure the safety of our clients, the proper execution of the exercises, and loading of the muscular structures. To take it a step further, when fatigue begins to accumulate on a movement and the subject voluntarily increases their effort, the body perceives this as an attempt to speed up. So the trainee's intent will actually be to move faster despite not being able to because of the fatigue. It is this effort and intent to keep one's pace despite the slowing movement that creates mechanical tension and ultimately the stimulus we seek from resistance training. See also Intent, Pace, and Tension.

Stretch - aside from the obvious meaning of the word stretch as most have come to the conclusion to describe the static act of lengthening a muscle, we have a slightly different use here. For our purposes, we refer to the stretched portion of a range of motion of an exercise as either exceeding the muscle's normal position/length at rest or the lengthening phase of movement. So during the lowering of a weight, or the eccentric, the muscle fibers are in fact lengthening as the degree of contraction is lessening.

Static Hold - a closely related method of static strength training to a Timed Static Contraction (TSC) but not as conservative, is the Static Hold (SH). While safer than dynamic exercise, it is potentially more risky than a TSC because during a Static Hold, the subject is actually holding or supporting a load. Whereas during a TSC, the subject is producing their own level of force against a movement arm that is locked in place and cannot be moved. Similar to the TSC, a Static Hold can be used in situations where a client is dealing with an injury, pain, discomfort, or a return from a surgical procedure. Static Holds have the benefit of objective feedback in the form of the load being held and the duration of the hold and as such, this method is more easily progressed. Additionally, since a Static Hold involves weight, there must be an interpersonal transfer of the load to and from the client, which requires extreme care and attention to detail. See the Static Hold module under the "Variations" section later in the Academy for more detail.

Tension (also Mechanical Tension or Muscular Tension) - refers to the degree or magnitude of stress experienced by activated muscle fibers under load. As a muscle contracts its muscle fibers grab and overlap along their length creating a pulling force on the bones/joints to which they are attached. Mechanical or muscular tension is the primary driving force, or stimulus, in the hypertrophic response that we seek from resistance training.

Timed Static Contraction (TSC) - as the name implies, a Timed Static Contraction (TSC) is an approach to strength training that involves producing an effort without movement. As such, it is typically safer than a dynamic exercise and can be a good option in situations where a client is dealing with an injury, pain, discomfort, or a return from a surgical procedure. The primary differentiator to a TSC is that there is no actual load being held or supported making it quite possibly the safest way to strength train. In order to perform a TSC, there needs to be an immovable movement arm to apply an effort against. This requires setting a given machine so that the movement arm is in the desired position of the range of motion and is held in place either by an amount of weight that cannot be lifted or with a selector pin that abuts the frame and prevents concentric movement. See the TSC module under the "Variations" section later in the Academy for more detail.

True Muscular Failure - training to the point where positive (concentric) movement is no longer possible due to muscular or central nervous system fatigue. While the phrase "true muscular failure" is still used in strength training circles is a technically inaccurate term. It is essentially impossible to recruit all of one's available muscle fibers and exhaust their strength through effort. It will most certainly come down to perceived effort, which happens well before true muscular failure. Nevertheless, it is worth acknowledging and distinguishing here as an instructor will likely hear this term at some point in their career. See also Failure and Fatigue for more.

Upper Turnaround (Upper Turn) - the specific point in the execution of an exercise signifying the end of the concentric, or lifting phase of the range of motion. The term "upper" is in reference to the position of the weight stack at the completion of the concentric phase of a given exercise repetition (i.e. it will be "lifted up"). This is not to be confused with the position of the body during the movement. For example, in the pulldown exercise the upper turnaround would be when the arms (and movement arm of the machine) are at the lowest point, closer to the body. But this is the upper turnaround because it is the end of the concentric phase and the weight stack will be at it's uppermost point. On certain exercises, the upper turnaround may also include what's known as an end stop.

Volume - in the strength training realm, volume usually refers to the amount of work performed in a workout. Some will use a basic formula of sets times reps and others may use weight times sets times reps. In any case, it is ultimately a misleading or even useless metric as not all reps in a workout are productive or stimulative. For our purposes we acknowledge the term volume as it relates to our use of a "low volume" protocol whereby we typically perform only one set per exercise and usually no more than 5 or 10 exercises in a session.
Equipment Nomenclature
Accessory stack - on machines with two weight stacks, the accessory stack is the smaller set of weights with smaller increments (usually 2, 2.5, or 5 pounds).

Add-ons - separate weights not included as part of the weight stack itself used to make smaller progressions. These should be kept on the floor nearby but completely out of the way of any traffic patterns or foot placement.

Axis of rotation - refers to both the pivot point of a movement arm on a machine and the acted upon joint in the body. It more accurately describes the axis on a single joint or rotary exercise where only one joint in the body is moving.

Bushing (oil impregnated bronze bushing) - refers to the small round "washer-like" part that acts as a cushion or liner for areas where metal passes through metal in order to reduce friction. In our case with the Imagine Strength equipment, most machines will have 4 of these, two for each of the weight stacks. There will be one bushing at the top of the frame of the weight stack and one at the bottom of the frame. These will be bronze in color and it is what the stack pin passes through. Every effort should be made to keep these junctions clean, with a thin film of lubricant on the stack pin. With use over time, the bushing will seep the oil and form to the stack pin to help maintain a friction free movement.
Carriage - essentially a larger 'movement arm' that encompasses or engages the torso, as seen on the Lumbar and Torso Rotation machines.

End Stop - a physical termination or abutment point strategically set on a machine that coincides with, or becomes, the upper turnaround in the execution of an exercise. The purpose of an end stop is to either prevent the limbs of the body from completely straightening and unloading, as would be used on a leg press, or to provide a point to apply effort against to increase the sensation of a muscular contraction, as could be used in a compound row or leg extension. In some cases, an end stop can be set to limit the range of motion of an exercise where a subject may be experiencing pain or that is contraindicated because of an injury. So for instance, if a client were to have shoulder pain closer to the lockout position of an overhead press, we could place a selector pin in the stack pin to create an end stop thereby preventing the client from lifting to full extension. See also Upper Turnaround.

Gap - the distance the movement arm is advanced before the weight is pinned on a selectorized machine. The gap is set to customize the lower turnaround on an exercise. The larger the gap that is used, the shorter the range of motion will be. A gap should be considered on most exercises for most clients to establish a safe and functional range of motion. For those trainees with an injury or some form of compromise, a properly set gap may allow them to use an exercise pain free that would otherwise be contraindicated.
Main stack - the primary weight stack on a machine with 2 weight stacks. The main stack will have the bigger plates with larger increments.

Movement Arm (or Work Arm) - the component or lever of the machine that is moved or lifted/lowered during the execution of an exercise. It will have either handles to grab or pads to push against when exercising. The movement arm then drives the weight stack through one or more articulations by either a lever(s), cable(s), or belt(s).

Range of Motion (of machine) - How far a machine's movement arm (and ultimately weight stack) moves during an exercise and the path that it tracks through. Most of the equipment we have will NOT be used through it's most fully possible range of motion. Each machine's range of motion should be customized to every individual client by using gaps and end stops to ensure safety and functionality. See also gap and end stop.
Selector pin - the pin used to select the amount of weight used on a given exercise. The selector pin goes under the weight and through a hole in the stack pin. See also stack pin.

Stack pin - the large metal rod that runs down through the center of the weight stack on a piece of selectorized equipment. The stack pin has holes in it that align with the holes in the weight plates that receive the selector pin when setting the weight to be used. Importantly, the stack should be kept clean with a lint free rag and a metal lubricant (TFL preferably) as needed but at least weekly. Where the stack pin passes through the bushings in the frame is one of the few possible points of friction and keeping the stack pin clean will help minimize this friction.

The exercise protocol and methods used at MaxStrength Fitness are an evolution of the Nautilus high-intensity training principles of Arthur Jones, the inventor of Nautilus exercise equipment. Of the various conflicting exercise theories and fads that have come and gone over the years, the principles of high-intensity training remain the most consistent with scientific research and the understanding of physiology. Accordingly, MSF’s approach to resistance training incorporates the most relevant literature that aligns with time-proven, fundamental exercise principles and physiological outcomes .

As you proceed through this manual, you will be introduced to the theory and principles of our Continuous Tension Method, the exercise protocol used at MaxStrength Fitness. You will also learn how to apply them in the design and instruction of effective, efficient, and safe exercise programs. Developing a thorough understanding of the material in this manual, in addition to the experience gained from your attention to detail over time, will ultimately lead you to become a master level, highly valued and sought after, strength training professional. While your first read through this conceptual framework may leave you with a multitude of questions, trust that this will all begin to come together as you learn the application side of our profession.
MaxStrength Fitness helps busy adults be healthy, fit, and strong in only twenty minutes twice a week without breaking a sweat.
This mission defines the operational standard for every MSF location and every client interaction. It establishes several non-negotiable priorities:
Time efficiency

MSF training is intentionally designed to produce meaningful results with minimal time commitment. This reflects an understanding of human physiology, where high effort and mechanical tension—not duration or volume—drive strength adaptation.
High-intensity strength training
Intensity refers to effort, not speed or exhaustion. MSF training emphasizes controlled, high-effort muscular work that can only be sustained briefly and must therefore be carefully coached.
Post-rehabilitation integration

MSF programming is appropriate for clients returning from injury or surgery due to its controlled execution, conservative ranges of motion, and emphasis on safety. This positions MSF uniquely between traditional fitness and clinical environments.
Professional delivery
Sessions are led by trained Exercise Practitioners who understand physiology, execution standards, and client communication. This reinforces trust, consistency, and outcomes.
Clinically controlled facilities
Equipment selection, setup, pacing, and supervision are all designed to minimize risk while maximizing stimulus. Safety is not a secondary benefit—it is a foundational requirement.
This mission clarifies that MSF is not a gym, a class-based model, or an entertainment-driven fitness experience. It is a professional strength training service.
Vision

MaxStrength Fitness will profoundly improve the quality of life for thousands of Americans by educating, inspiring and providing the most efficient, effective and safe strength training program ever created. Our employees will be life changers and will have extensive growth opportunities while fulfilling their passion and servicing their clients.
The MSF vision expands beyond workouts and locations. It defines the long-term impact of the organization on clients, employees, and communities.
Improving quality of life
Increased strength improves independence, resilience, injury resistance, and confidence. MSF training is positioned as a long-term health solution, not a short-term fitness trend.
Education and inspiration
MSF does not simply deliver exercise; it teaches clients how and why strength training works. This educational component increases adherence, trust, and long-term success.
Efficiency, effectiveness, and safety as core values
The vision reinforces that these three elements are inseparable. Removing any one of them compromises the program.
Employees as life changers

MSF Exercise Practitioners are not task supervisors. They are professionals who guide clients through a challenging and transformative process. Their ability to coach effort, intent, and execution directly influences outcomes.
Growth and fulfillment

The vision recognizes that sustained excellence depends on developing skilled, motivated professionals. MSF is committed to creating meaningful career paths while allowing practitioners to pursue their passion for helping others.

For franchise owners, the mission and vision provide a clear lens through which all decisions should be made—staffing, training, client experience, and operational standards. They define what MSF is, what it is not, and why consistency in execution matters.

topics.title: Strength Training at MSF
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 1 - Introduction/Academy - Intro 5 - Strength Training at MSF.txt

blocks.text: Contrary to public perception about the role of a “personal trainer”, this isn’t just a job where you teach exercise. It is a role built on human connection, trust, and responsibility. As an Exercise Practitioner with MSF, you will work with people from every background, personality type, and life circumstance. Some will be confident, others intimidated. Some will be disciplined, others inconsistent. Many will bring stress, frustration, fear, or past failure into the session with them. Your ability to recognize this and respond appropriately is not optional, it is foundational.

At its core, leading someone through a physically challenging endeavor is one of the highest forms of human interaction. Our clients are not just paying for a workout. They are placing trust in you to guide them, understand them, and motivate them. That requires integrity, a relentless work ethic, and the ability to model the discipline and habits you expect from others.

You must be able to communicate clearly, but more importantly, you must be able to listen with intent. If you cannot connect with a client, you cannot coach them effectively, regardless of how strong your technical knowledge may be.

Yes, you are expected to develop expert-level understanding of anatomy, exercise, and the MSF Continuous Tension Protocol. But knowledge alone does not make you effective. Your success will ultimately be determined by your ability to apply that knowledge through the lens of empathy, adaptability, and real human interaction.

Exercise Instruction isn't just about taking clients through workouts. It's about building relationships, adhering to principles, and looking for opportunities to always be teaching. It's much more than simply making people work hard. The Academy and its multitude of appendices will teach you how to apply our protocol, but what cannot be taught is how to naturally and effectively interact with people. The clients need to sense our passion. This ability is essential to creating relationships with clients and earning their trust.

The material contained in this course, as well as the practical scripts and other resources, will provide a wealth of knowledge that should be used as the basis for intelligent and meaningful interactions with clients. These modules will inform you how to discuss exercise…the “personal touch” will be up to you.

Keep this in mind...the clients won't care how much we know until they know how much we care. As trite as that may sound, consider how true that is for you personally in your experiences with others. Now realize how impactful it can be when you truly take an interest in another person and how that helps build a strong relationship and level of trust. And also keep in mind that this is an elevated experience at MSF and the client is paying a premium. We should be providing MORE in value than the client is making in payment. This is one of our core values and quite possibly the most important one…Overdeliver!

topics.title: Posture, Path, Pace, Purpose
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 1 - Introduction/Academy - Intro 6 - Posture, Path, Pace, Purpose.txt

blocks.text: The 4 P's - Posture, Pace, Path, Purpose - What to look for at a high level when instructing or performing proper resistance training.
POSTURE

Every exercise has a "get set" (i.e. starting position) and regardless of how long a client has been with us, we need to properly position them. This can be as brief as a phrase or two or as involved as a detailed explanation if need be. Newer clients will obviously need more instruction but even an advanced client might benefit from a reminder of "how" and "why" we should be positioned to avoid falling into casual rehearsed patterns. Keep in mind, the more we can teach and explain our methods to a client the more likely we are to appear as experts and keep our clients engaged. That reasoning aside, it is even more important from a safety and effectiveness standpoint to ensure the client is properly positioned. An exercise is only ever as good as the setup and oftentimes the "get set" and the ability to maintain that posture throughout the movement determines what receives the loading and therefore the stimulus. Regardless of what sensations are "felt" during the movement.

A majority of our exercises are either performed with a "chest up" posture, so anterior pelvic tilt, or a poster pelvic tilt where the abdomen is held in the contracted position. Both of these postures should set the ribcage in a stable position, which means there should be no change in the position of the torso for the duration of the movement. Consider it part of the exercise and look to preemptively remind the clients during their execution of the exercise.

Also included under the Posture category is the idea of proper bracing. Without proper bracing, the subject will not be able to continuously produce enough of a leveraged effort to create a stimulus. This is also why maintaining proper posture and bracing throughout the set is just as important as being properly set up at the beginning of the exercise. The instructor should continue to cue proper posture and bracing during the movement. Any sort of collapse, shifting, or wiggling poses an energy leak, which leads to a decreased output and unloading of targeted muscle groups. And as we know, we need an increasing output and continuous tension over the course of a set, which is only possible through proper posture and bracing. For an advanced subject, this becomes even more paramount in terms of attempting to truly progress. In the worst case scenario, any form of postural shift while under load can pose a risk of injury. This alone should be enough of a motivation to remain properly positioned and the trainer should warn of this to improve compliance.

As a general observation, if the subject can manage to keep their head and ribcage still (or the relationship between the head and ribcage constant), many of the other common discrepancies we see will take care of themselves and the targeted muscles will stand a better chance of experiencing mechanical tension.
PACE

A smooth, continuous speed of movement will help to ensure safe and effective resistance training. Limiting momentum will allow us to use less weight and afford the client a better opportunity to exact control of the movement. Keep in mind that the better a subject controls the weight, the more tension the muscles will experience. This increased tension, while desirable for purposes of creating a stimulus, will also increase the subjects' perception of effort. Most of our clients (and the general population for that matter) will associate this struggle and resulting perception of effort with an undesirable or overwhelming feeling. But this "feeling" IS an indicator of the stimulus we seek. The event we're trying to create through resistance training is the very thing that our nervous systems instinctively looks to protect us from in the form of afferent feedback.

So as fatigue begins to accumulate and the muscle's contraction velocity slows during an exercise (as evidenced by the machine's movement arm bogging down), the trainee experiences more and more discomfort. The true challenge and focus should be to MAINTAIN THEIR PACE, which is only accomplished through an increasing effort (i.e. pushing or pulling harder). So by encouraging and reinforcing the concept of maintaining their pace, we may be able to shift the focus from the accumulating discomfort and simplify the task of increasing one's effort. While it is important for us to remind our clients what the muscular target is in an exercise, this may be counterproductive as they approach muscular failure. A simple shift in focus to keeping a constant pace may allow the subject to push closer to failure with better quality.

For those clients that are more intensity adverse, heavier loads and a faster pace (closer to 6 seconds than 10) may help minimize discomfort while still achieving the desired stimulus. This should only be implemented to the degree that the client displays proper understanding and execution and should be introduced progressively. Newer trainees or those who are more deconditioned will most likely benefit from training with lighter loads and a slower pace.

So to summarize, a good way to teach our clients to train harder with more effort when it is needed most is to challenge them to maintain their pace throughout the set. This will actually require them to go from moving slowly at the onset to speeding up at some point during the exercise. The trainer needs to become acutely aware of this and be able to anticipate the need for proper instruction at the right time.
PATH

The next consideration in the 4 P's would be Path. Path refers to the plane of motion, or movement pattern, followed by a limb, or in some cases the torso or head, during the execution of a given exercise. Because the body automatically detects and recruits the muscles with the best line of pull and leverage in a given body position, the path we use will determine what muscle fibers will be activated (neuromechanical matching). On certain exercises, the path may not be able to be varied or changed. The more locked in or restrained a subject is, the less variability in the path of execution there can be (think lumbar extension for example). But for many exercises, especially upper body movements, the limb's path will be a determining factor in the leverage or bias a particular muscle fiber has at a particular joint angle. This ultimately affects which muscle fibers actually receive the stimulus (tension).

Let's consider the compound row as an example. If we begin a set by carrying the elbows out wide relative to the torso (abducted) and then begin to tuck the elbows closer to the torso as we fatigue (adduct), we are essentially performing a different exercise. If our goal is to create as much tension in a muscle or muscle group then we want to keep those same muscles under continuous tension throughout the entire exercise. By changing the angle of the arm/elbow we shift the tension away from the target to different muscles. Yes, the back muscles in general will still be loaded but the primary movers will change from the upper back to the lats.

This is one of the more challenging aspects of proper training for a newer trainee to overcome. Instinctively the body will attempt to find the path of least resistance. The client will be operating under the premise of the assumed objective; to keep the machine moving as long as they can. In order to do this, they will need to unload what is fatiguing or uncomfortable and transfer the effort to other muscles. Again, this is a built-in feature of the body that acts as a protective mechanism to help ensure survival. In order for resistance training to be effective, one needs to learn to overcome this instinctive measure and be continuous with their effort. They must understand the muscles are still capable of producing force despite the discomfort they are experiencing.

Here is another example where our communication, instruction, and preemptive cueing set us apart from other trainers that merely count reps. We need to be able to anticipate the likely training discrepancies and help keep our clients in the safest and most beneficial positions to ensure successful workouts. With our own practical training experience, we're able to put ourselves in the subjects' shoes on a moment-to-moment basis and give timely, objective, and informative instruction.
PURPOSE

The 4th and final P in our MSF Instructor "cheat sheet" is Purpose. Simply stated, the purpose of training is to become more tolerant of training (and essentially, getting better at training). This may very well be the missing ingredient to most attempts at a productive and successful exercise intervention. Purpose is essentially addressing the question, 'what is the primary or immediate goal of our exercise?'. The technical answer to this is an increase in Motor Unit Recruitment (MUR), which leads to a greater number of muscle fibers exposed to mechanical tension, which leads to a more meaningful stimulus. In order to increase MUR over time, the trainee must learn to train harder and be more tolerant of the effort required. But this is not an instinctive measure for most. Instinctively, most people are merely trying to hang-on or survive when they train. Instead, subjects would be better served to focus on maintaining their posture, their pace, and their path. Additionally, if the subject can learn to progress their intensity/effort while maintaining the other 3 P's they are well on their way to mastery. But how exactly do we teach a client to change their intent during such an arduous and uncomfortable task? The short answer is continual practice accompanied by timely instruction. And while Behavioral Science is an entirely different field of study that is beyond our expertise as instructors, we can lean on some basic principles. Rather than focusing on the discomfort or the struggle, the instructor should empower the client to focus on perfecting their exercise execution. This includes how well they organize their body and control the movement. In many ways our Continuous Tension protocol can be compared to practicing a martial art, where there is a strong qualitative and introspective approach. It's safe to say that for most, this attribute is missing from their exercise. The fight or flight instinct is extremely strong and well preserved in our species. It takes a concerted effort to try and overcome or at least temporarily "dupe" these mechanisms. And this understanding is another competitive advantage or differentiator that MSF Instructors hold over the rest of the industry. Our insight and our instruction provide meaningful value to our client's and their fitness journeys.
CONCLUSION

As you read through the MSF Academy you will come to learn that there are plenty of other factors to consider on our journey of mastering our craft as Exercise Practitioners. But these 4 principles should be constantly monitored and used to properly inform our clients to focus on a more qualitative effort. This is the key to productive high-intensity training.

By keeping mind the 4 P's of effective resistance training, and continuously instructing within this framework, we are better able to hold our clients accountable to their effort and quality. We are also more likely to achieve a level of consistency among trainers. And of even greater importance, by implementing the concepts discussed here and throughout the MSF Academy, we are given the opportunity to demonstrate to our clients that we care more about their workouts than they do. Our clients will feel as though they could not train this way or go through these workouts on their own. And at the end of the day, the success of our business is determined almost entirely by the clients' perceived quality of the workouts, which are performed one repetition at a time.
**ALSO SEE THE MSF MASTERY SERIES FOR MORE INSIGHT INTO THE 4 P's OF RESISTANCE TRAINING AND OTHER QUALITATIVE TRAINING TOPICS.

topics.title: Random Notes and FAQs
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 1 - Introduction/Academy - Intro 7 - Random Notes and FAQ_s.txt

blocks.text: One of the biggest challenges we will face as Exercise Practitioners at MSF is attempting to explain to someone what we do and to convince them that it is “enough” activity to be a complete strength training program. This will likely not be an issue when we have them in the studio for a consultation. They will get to try the workout firsthand, which is usually enough to get the point across. The challenge will be for those that call in to inquire or for those conversations we find ourselves in outside of the studio. For this reason, it helps to have a bit of a script prepared and to remember a few key selling points. Our brand script is a very useful tool in these situations: “We help men and women reverse the aging process in only 20 minutes twice a week without breaking a sweat. Because everyone deserves to be healthy, fit and strong without wasting hours in the gym”! You’ll notice that in these two sentences we have highlighted the main benefits of the protocol. There are certain features of the protocol that help further explain what we do, like continuous tension, slow, controlled movement, high intensity effort, temperature controlled room, specialized equipment specific to our protocol, one on one expert trainers, etc. But it is important to lead with the benefits, that’s what will matter most to prospective clients.

Quite possibly the most important skill that an Exercise Practitioner can have as they master their craft, would be the ability to communicate. Now, it should go without saying that being an empathetic listener is critical in making that human connection with our clients too. But in most cases, the communication will go one way during the workout - from Instructor to client (or at least it should). And that communication needs to be something other than discussing the Instructor's personal life or counting reps or duration of squeezes or "cheerleading". Yes there is a place for well timed encouragement but it should always be at a reasonable volume and done with a calm delivery.

The communication referred to here would be that which conveys the value of the workout. Read that last sentence again. We need to develop the ability to discuss the details of our protocol in a way that is direct, concise, actionable, and value added. In other words, our clients need to be beyond convinced that we are passionate and knowledgeable about resistance training and our enthusiasm needs to come through our instruction. And it shouldn't feel forced or be overtly demonstrative. It should be genuine, organic, and conversational…eventually. The “conversation” is the actionable instruction and internal guidance we are providing. Both external and internal cues. Our clients are paying us for our words. The MSF Exercise Practitioner should be diligent in pursuing mastery of their craft - communication. Most of what an Instructor might want to say during a session in the form of instruction can be found throughout the MSF Academy and our Equipment Scripts. And because of this, the instructor should continually refer back to these resources to further equip their experience with insight.

Importantly, we need to acknowledge that some of our clients will "get it" while others will not. For those that aren't catching on to the intricacies of what we're trying to do, the instructors need to do more. Breakthroughs can happen with enough practice and the right words. Those 'right words' need to come from the instructor. Not everything we say will resonate the same with all clients, so we should constantly seek a better explanation. Or the most helpful discussion to have. Sometimes just reframing the Real Objective (Purpose) can have the impact that's needed. So reminding the client that we're seeking 'the path of most resistance' or that we're trying to create an 'intentional struggle' will get them to begin to see the qualitative side that we're seeking. Remember, this is a learning process for both sides. Just as the client can get better with their technique, we can get better with our observations and instruction. So be diligent in looking for new ways to communicate. This is also a surefire way to improve client retention.
Remember, it should be apparent to the client that their instructor cares more about the workout than they do!

Keep in mind, that on top of the 4 P's discussed in the module above, our clients will also need to be reminded to relax their face and jaw and to breathe freely. Oftentimes when a client holds their breath or tenses up their face, it is accompanied by a movement discrepancy, usually in the form of a heave or lunge or some sort of sudden movement. This again is evidence that they are operating instinctively under the ASSUMED OBJECTIVE (see glossary). The instructor needs to be attentive and proactive to anticipate these actions as we do not want them to become habitual. Remember, this is a journey and we are teaching our clients how to train Safely and Effectively. Therefore, we need to correct and instruct with this in mind. In fact, this cueing can be easily added in combination with other effort-based cues for those that are likely offenders. For instance, we can blend together, "head still...keep breathing...pull harder". So we have qualitative reminders with encouragement all in one, concise phrase. These combinations can be very useful especially if they are well timed. This is a great way for a novice instructor to evolve and grow - strive for cues that are meaningful, helpful, and timely.

If there was only one thing we could do to ensure the quality of a set of exercise, it would be to emphasize the Lower Turnaround!!! The simplest way to control a client's movement with the least amount of verbiage or cueing is to require strict, exaggerated control of the lower turnaround. This is easier said than done however as this tends to be the most challenging position mechanically on most exercises. And this is not to say that we should be using the least amount of cueing but rather to point out how much of the movement quality is entirely attributable to the execution of the lower turnaround.

We are responsible for the success of the client's workouts. We are the experts. If a client is struggling with control or if there's clear evidence that the load may be too heavy, adjust the weight. If they finish their set and comment that it "wasn't good" and you also noticed that it "wasn't good" please give them another opportunity to make it good. Now, we don't want to make a habit of doing more sets to make up for the lack of quality but if the weight is too heavy or the client is just having an off day, we should make the necessary adjustment so that they don't leave disappointed. It also gives us another chance to reinforce the concepts (4 P's maybe) that they are not grasping. Think of it as a fresh start where you can get a different level of engagement and focus from the client. Lower the weight, communicate your expectations, and challenge them to a more qualitative effort. Then take the opportunity to discuss how it went afterwards.

In conjunction with the other points listed, the instructor should be constantly evaluating the machine settings as we observe our client's training. This one may not be as obvious for a newer trainer, but there may be opportunities to optimize an exercise just based on the settings alone. When clients are injured or are dealing with discomfort in a joint, we are quick to modify the settings to ensure they can keep training. But there are instances where everything seems fine training-wise and there are no apparent issues that would require changing the settings. However, after a client has been on a machine and progressed in weight, their alignment may have changed. Also keep in mind that changing the settings may be used as a form of progression. For instance, if you have a client who just keeps increasing weight and reps on a leg press we may want to consider lowering the weight and creating a deeper lower turnaround. Just one setting deeper can make the exercise feel new again. Or maybe going from a more laid back position on leg press, which is more quadriceps biased to a more upright position, which is more hip biased. Sometimes just raising or lowering the seat on a chest press will create a better path and more leverage as the humerus adducts into the pectorals (SAME BUT DIFFERENT). One more example might be the relationship of the footplate and the femur restraint on the lumbar and abdominal. What tends to happen over time as the weights increase, the clients push harder into the footplate, which is to be expected. By pushing harder, they sink into the pads more and the knee is allowed to straighten further. Before you know it, the knee is no longer above the head of the femur at the hip, which is the positioning we want. In this case, we may find the need to bring the footplate in one setting closer. Along with that, the femur restraint will most likely need to come in closer too. This can only be found by the trainer squatting down during the client's set and observing the joint alignment.

Try not to involve the client at all with rep counts, weights, or the process of setting up of machines. They do not need to know any of this and it only complicates things for future workouts. Now obviously there are exceptions but be aware of unnecessary or rambling explanations and look to avoid them. Instead, use the time you are setting them up or loading/unloading to bring their awareness back to the REAL OBJECTIVE of resistance training. Give them feedback on what they just did or what they're about to do. Or teach them something about why we are cueing certain things or how a particular exercise will benefit them. Constantly reinforcing quality execution. This is a value-added way to continue to "sell" to them and position ourselves as experts. Anything else becomes confusing, noisy chatter and may give the client reasons to doubt our abilities.

There seems to be this pervasive thought among clients that we are in the position of being some sort of taskmaster and that they are being forced to lift more weight for more reps or even worse, "tortured". And it's always proclaimed in a lighthearted and playful manner, oftentimes between the clients as they interact in the lobby. In a way, it becomes something that they can bond (i.e. commiserate) over. Any attempt to remind them of our role and what we are really trying to accomplish is usually met with the customary, "Oh I know...I was kidding". But unfortunately, they still do not truly understand the nature of the relationship. Strength training has been scientifically proven to be one of the most valuable interventions one can partake in to improve health and longevity. But this training has to be of a high intensity and a near maximal effort, especially for those that are beyond the novice level. Just moving the machine and going through the motions is not enough to create an effect. The intensity required is not something most could ever accomplish on their own. Our clients should realize that this is an extremely challenging endeavor and that we are there to assist and ensure they are creating the desired stimulus.

"Did you add weight?" This is probably the most frequently asked client question. In some cases, you may decide that it's completely acceptable to answer with a 'yes' or 'no' to your more experienced clients. And even a newer client might be best advised to hear something along the lines of, "yes that was more weight this time, but we raise the weights for most of our clients over time as they learn how to do this." Importantly, we need to always remember to frame our response within the proper context of the REAL OBJECTIVE. So while they may have noticed the increased weight, what is more important is that we comment on their movement quality. Remind them that the weight is the least important of the variables and that adding weight is a last resort of progression. We are much more concerned and focused on their quality; proper posture, head still, face relaxed, gradual load up, breathing freely, controlled pace, continuous change of direction, increased breathing with effort, etc. All of these factors are more important to creating mechanical tension (i.e. the stimulus) than the weight itself. Remind them that they are attempting to maximize the tension in the muscles, which is a completely different experience than seeing how much they can lift. And that every repetition of every exercise is a chance to begin to master a skill that can quite literally transform their life.

"I don't know..." is a perfectly acceptable answer to a client's question. We are frequently seen as experts of all things health-related to our clients. Quite often we will get questions outside of the strength training realm that we may not have a logical answer to given the nature of our place on the health and fitness spectrum. We may even get questions that are strength training or anatomy related that we're not confident in answering. In either case, it is best to say something along the lines of, "Good question, I don't know the answer to that but I'll look into it." Then make sure you actually look into it and get back to the client with some sort of value added feedback. Either inquire with the rest of the team or do some online research. A true expert knows what they don't know and will admit to it rather than just purely speculating to appear knowledgeable. The clients will appreciate this as you will most likely be able to more intelligently answer their questions or at least point them in the right direction. This is yet another example of our competitive advantage. As strength training professionals, we don't give typical "personal trainer" answers using outdated "gym logic".

Teaching HOW to squeeze and when to say it. Keep in mind that when we instruct an uninformed trainee to "squeeze" they will most likely clench their fists. It's the instinctive action that is most familiar in this case. And because we are always wanting to add value to a workout, we should describe to the client exactly HOW to squeeze the muscles we are targeting. An example would be to instruct the subject to continuously attempt to straighten (or over-straighten) their knee in the contracted or extended position of the leg extension. This is how an advanced trainer will differentiate themselves from a typical trainer that simply tells the client to squeeze.

"I don't feel my [insert muscle group], am I doing it wrong?" This is another common question we will get from clients. And as trainers, we should consider ourselves fortunate that we are getting this feedback. This is another opportunity for us to prove our worth! Another opportunity for the client to become dependent on our insight. But our insight needs to be truthful and informative. It's too easy to be dismissive here and that's what most trainers would do. We need to have genuine concern for the client's inquiries. It may very well be that they just need more time and more practice with their focus and technique. Or the musculature that we're attempting to target just is not as sensitive as others. For instance, the lats are significantly less sensitive than the thighs or the triceps. We should be able to confidently explain this. At the end of the day, if we have the client properly positioned and the movement path is accurate, we can be assured that the targeted musculature is the prime mover. And this should be the informed and intelligent discussion we have with the client. The ability to mentally connect with a muscle or to feel the working muscle is usually muscle group specific and is more importantly highly individualized. But it can also be progressed and improved upon over the course of a training career. And this is where our focus should be anyway. Our clients should be encouraged to progress their effort, quality, and focus over time. The quantitative measures of weight and reps are essentially meaningless at the level our clients are at, they need to focus on the 4 P's and we should instruct accordingly!

Aside from asking “was that more weight?”, asking, “am I getting stronger?”, seems to be one of the more frequently asked questions. And while we could simply answer yes or no…they would most likely require further explanation to satisfy them. With this being the case, a little background information is necessary for perspective.

Firstly, anyone engaging in a properly designed, safely performed, progressively challenged strength training program can expect to get stronger. This is especially true for those that haven't done any sort of strength training in the recent past. So most assuredly we can answer “yes” to that inquiry. But the reason they are asking must be because they are unaware themselves or need to be convinced. This is an unfortunate occurrence.

It could be that the person asking lives a relatively inactive life, in which case they would not have an opportunity to notice or prove to themselves that they have in fact gotten stronger. Again, this is unfortunate but probably not that uncommon. But if this is the case, then any amount of strength training done with any level of intensity should represent a profound “wake up call” of sorts. Or it could be that this particular individual is just physically unaware of themselves, which would tend to be the case for a good number of our clients as that is what possibly drew them to MSF in the first place. In other words, they don’t know how to tell or measure their new levels of strength and want an objective measurement from the workout chart. While the answer would be, “yes, you are lifting more weight than you did when you started,” that can be a little misleading.

It can almost be guaranteed that one will go on to lift more weight at MSF than when they first joined. Part of the reason is because we will start conservatively with them, using significantly lighter weights than they are currently capable of lifting to facilitate the learning process. It takes time and attention to learn how to properly strength train and our focus is always on the qualitative approach. So the relative light weights that we start with will soon be surpassed as the client learns how to control their movement and effort. In this case, it is likely that they have gotten stronger as the neurological adaptations alone that take place very quickly, on a rep-to-rep basis at times, are a big component of getting stronger. On a side note, strength itself is not an adaptation, but rather an outcome. There are 6 or more adaptations that go into making someone stronger of which neurological efficiency and muscle mass are two of the major ones.

Now in the case of an advanced client that has been training for 3 - 5 years or more, there is a chance that they have reached their genetic “ceiling” in terms of strength. In fact everyone is likely to reach this point if they subject themselves to enough stimulus (i.e. training sessions). But once we reach this point, it would make zero sense to stop training as we would then begin to lose our strength. So it’s best to just keep training without concern for a genetic limit. Just assume that it doesn’t even exist, keep training, and at least maintain as much strength as you can for the rest of your life.

All of that to say that the real bottleneck in all of this usually comes down to the willingness or tolerance of the client to produce a truly hard and adaptive effort. When someone first begins a strength training program (or any physical activity for that matter), almost everything will be stimulative as it will be at a level above what they are currently used to. However, as one gets stronger, the current level of effort will not be enough to surpass the newfound level of strength. A harder, more intense effort is required to keep progressing. This is a simple biological adaptation model. The more someone has engaged in training, the higher the level of output is required to be stimulative. But the good news is, with more training comes more ability and tolerance and skill. The subject should be capable of training harder because of the practice of training and the instruction they receive. This is the primary purpose of an Exercise Practitioner. Aside from ensuring their safety of course.

There should be no doubt to the subject that they themselves have gotten stronger if they are consistently training with us and they are focused on their intensity and technique. They should be able to feel the difference proper strength training makes by just standing there with an awareness. If not and we need to point to other examples, we have gotten plenty of input over the years:
Posture
Less joint pain
Getting out of bed
Up and down stairs
Getting in and out of the car
Golfing
Carrying groceries
Lifting up children
Yardwork
Opening doors
Walking through stores or the neighborhood
Loading/unloading items from the trunk
Getting off the floor
Getting out of a chair
Lifting suitcase into overhead storage

All of these would be indicative of an increase in strength. They are all also improved with practice as any physical endeavor is specific. If one wants to get better at going up and down stairs or getting off the floor, these should be carefully practiced. The strength increase will make all of those things easier but the point being that there is also a skill component.

So to sum up, yes, everyone that begins training with us will assuredly become stronger. The question is, how much and to what degree? And this is entirely up to the individual. How seriously will they take their sessions and the instruction? How much will they challenge themselves to get better at strength training? The Instructor will not hold them back and they will even encourage, but ultimately it is up to the client to decide how hard they want to work over time. In this way, they will not ever have to question whether they are getting stronger, they will give their body no choice.
